Employer context reached this public repository and is out of every page at HEAD. Four pages carried it, and the worst was not the one that raised the question: GitHub/Action/Runner/ARM/Concept/Overview of Cost and Deployment held seven footnote links into a private AI workspace, and had since 2025-07-22.
A rewrite changes every commit hash, and this graph cites its own hashes in prose, so it would break its own references. Existing clones and forks keep the old objects regardless.

Three agent-written narrative blocks were deleted by hand from the 2026-08-18 Tue journal, and a top-level block in Person/codekiln's own voice was added above that day's Filed hours later. Prose in a journal is not evidence that anything went wrong; the seat writes only the change log and neither writes nor removes the narrative.

My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff was a third page teaching the deleted practice and no longer is. That much was already a decision on record, so it was brought into line rather than asked about. The two remaining pages state the convention itself, which is not the seat's to change.

The books are at the flat Book/<title> path rather than the Book/YY/<short title> the entity definition points multi-author books at. That dated form has no instance in this graph — 33 flat book pages and 19 under a person, none dated — and the multi-author books already here, Book/Understanding by Design and Book/ML with PyTorch and Scikit-Learn, are both flat. Creating the first dated one would have set a convention.

On a flat page the year sits in date-created::, and the graph's habit there is the original publication year: Book/Understanding by Design carries 1998 though its expanded edition is 2005. So Book/The Elements of Style carries 1918, Strunk's own printing, with the 1959 revision by Person/E. B. White made prominent in the prose instead. One page rather than two, because the graph keeps one page per book and this is one work with a revision history.

Monks of New Skete is an Organization rather than a Person, so the collective author needed no new convention. created-by:: here already points at non-person bodies including LangChain, Google, Gitlab and IEEE/Committee/LTSC, and Logseq/Entity/Organization already had IETF and MITRE as instances. An alias:: line naming New Skete is suggested and unwritten, because aliases are human-curated.

Person/William Strunk Jr carries no trailing period. The period belongs to his name, and a page file ending in one would be this graph's first, which would make the title Logseq reads back from the filename disagree with every link written to it. The Wikipedia link on the page carries the punctuated form.

Two page paths inherited from the seat's own handoff were wrong and were corrected before being written into the book pages. Do not coin phrases unless asked and I am allergic to word salad live under My/AI/Rule/How to Communicate Effectively With Me/ rather than under My/Pref/Writing/; linking the handoff's version would have created two empty pages competing with real ones.

My/AI/Rule/How to Communicate Effectively With Me/Talk to me like a friend, not in vague aphorisms already cited both writing books before the import began and names them as the test a phrase should pass before it is written, so the reason for importing them was on record rather than inferred. Both book pages link back to it.

Thomas and Turner hold plain style apart from classic style, so My/Pref/Writing/Use Plain language and its readability targets sit closer to plain style than to the style their book argues for. The page says so rather than claiming the book underwrites measuring prose that way. Book/The Art of Raising a Puppy carries its bearing on agent work marked as a tentative reading, because Person/codekiln did not say why that book belongs with the two on writing.

lefthook.yml had declared the guard since 2026-06-10 and it had never once run, because lefthook install was never run in this clone, so .git/hooks held only stock samples. A committed hook config with no install is the default state of every fresh clone, since .git/hooks is not tracked. Read it with ls .git/hooks rather than by reading the config.

A whole-repo scan went from 60 findings in 18 files to none. Most of the 60 were never leaks: home paths in pages whose value is the copied output, and the employer named as a public fact about other people. Installing the guard as it stood would have blocked the seat's own handoff commit over a home path, which is how a guard earns a permanent bypass.

Six pages whose value is copied terminal output are named in .secretlintignore. Eight lines stating a third party's public affiliation carry an inline exemption with its reason beside it, rather than the whole page being silenced — three conference pages, a faculty profile and two verbatim public transcripts. Silencing a page to quiet a guard is the same mistake as a guard that cries wolf, reached from the other side.

Two inherited claims about the guard were verified rather than acted on, and both needed it. An in-file exemption written with a colon before its reason is ignored, where -- before the reason works. An exemption on a file's last line is ignored when the file has no trailing newline, which was true of 491 of 800 pages sampled here. Both produce an exemption that reads as applied, shows correctly in a diff, and does nothing. Annotate, then re-scan the file.

Redacted at HEAD where it cost nothing and rewritten where it cost something. The ARM footnotes cited public sources but linked private conversations no reader could open, so naming each original lost nothing. The browser profile table on My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Browser was rewritten rather than removed, because an instruction in use depends on it.

Leaving the account addresses off that page was the right call scoped to the wrong unit, which is why the page still leaked: it withheld the addresses and published the domain, and the domain is the employer. No word list would have caught it, because the guard's list did not carry the university name either.

The Harvard Art Museums article title stayed on archive.ph while the institutional-access phrasing came off. A public article about an institution is not an affiliation; the guard cannot tell those apart and a person can.

72e3b4aa swept two of Person/codekiln's own edits into a commit under this seat's message and co-author trailer. Staging named paths protects against other files rather than against a second writer in the same file; the missing check was git diff --cached before committing. It was left alone because rewriting a pushed public branch over a trailer costs more than the inconsistency.
A peer seat's tmux/Option/pane-border-* pages were left alone. They are that seat's work in a shared checkout, and reaching into them is what handing over exists to avoid.
The 24 slash-form date links on pages written that day were left alone. Logseq/Date calls [[YYYY/MM/DD]] acceptable and merely not preferred for new writes, so rewriting committed ones is churn.

CursorAI/Explanation/Grok Bot on a Teams seat answers the billing question: a Teams seat includes access at no extra charge on Standard as well as Premium, with no admin action needed. Grok Bot is xAI's agent application, neither Cursor's Bugbot reviewer nor the Grok models, and the page separates all three because they bill differently. What can still cost money is usage rather than access.

archive.ph worked on a paywalled Boston Globe article, recorded as a dated attributed test because everything else on that page was written 2025-10-05 Sun and never revisited. It does not settle the institutional-access route, which is a different mechanism.

The tmux session-name probe was re-run rather than published from the note already written, and it needed re-running: the original test used session:0 targets, the one target form a dot in the name leaves alone. The finding is now tmux/Q/Why does a session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?.

Lazygit/Q/Can an agent open lazygit on one file in one commit for me to review? settles how an agent hands over a review: lazygit --filter <path> opens on the commit with the diff restricted to that path, and a detached git/worktree at an older commit puts it first in the list.

Work in My/Knowledge/Garden/logseq-encode-garden that Hayward went looking for and found, where the next step is a decision rather than more measuring. My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/LEG Todos Heads Up Display holds what Person/codekiln asked for; this page holds what nobody has asked for yet.
The order below is Hayward's guess at your priority, and that guess is the only thing ranking these. current-as-of:: above is the governing time.

First day of a chief-of-staff agent in this graph. herdr workspace w2 ran encode-garden-chief-of-staff while chiefs over other repos ran in the same herdr instance, which is what makes <workspace>-chief-of-staff enough of a name to find every one of them without a roster.

A chief absorbs a subagent's findings, not only its questions. A long, well-organized briefing that arrives with its decisions already made is the weeds moved rather than cleared, and being correct, complete, and legible is no defense.

The check before reporting: what decision does this need from the human? What turns on no decision gets digested to its outcome, or left out. A verification trail belongs on the page it verified, not in the report.
What belongs in this graph, and what does not

This garden is public, and a chief reads other repos' panes all day. A repo name picked up that way is not knowledge about Person/codekiln — it is somebody else's private context passing through, and a page here is the wrong place for it. Write the pattern and leave the repo unnamed.
What belongs in this graph, and what does not

Three agents and the human were writing into the single checkout at ~/ghq/github.com/codekiln/logseq-encode-garden. encode-garden-scribe took the journal and the commits, and the agents writing pages handed files over rather than running git add themselves. One stager gives one commit per finished thing instead of a sweep that bundles somebody else's half-written page.

Staging has an order as well as an owner. Reading a diff establishes what a file held at that moment, and git add runs after — so in a shared checkout an edit landing in between is committed unreviewed, and nothing reports it. Stage first, read git diff --cached, then commit, and the window closes.
Text in an input box is not the human

An idle agent may render a suggested follow-up where a typed line would sit, drawn from its own last turn. It is the machine talking to itself, and it is not evidence of human input in either direction — not consent, and not a reason to wait.
Text in an input box is not the human

The tell is the rendering, and it is a property of the content rather than of the box. Generated text is emitted dim, wrapped as ESC[2m … ESC[0m; text that arrived as real input carries no styling, and neither does an idle pane's empty box. So the test is that dim wrapper around content, never the presence or absence of styling — read it as "no styling means a human typed it" and an idle pane's empty box becomes human input. herdr agent read <name> --source visible --format ansi shows the wrapper; a plain-text read flattens it away.
Text in an input box is not the human

The give-away in the content is that each suggestion paraphrases the recommendation its own agent had just made. Six panes here carried one at once, each mirroring the report above it, and none of them were the human's. Six people do not half-type into six panes simultaneously, and the base rate was the cheapest check available.
Text in an input box is not the human

The box is drawn in every state. During a turn it is drawn empty, with its prompt marker coloured grey — ESC[38;2;153;153;153m — so a mid-turn read comes back blank because the box holds nothing, not because the box is missing. That grey marker is itself a tell: it separates a working pane's empty box from an idle one's, which carries no styling at all.
Text in an input box is not the human

An empty box otherwise says nothing. A suggestion may appear once an agent is idle or done, and often none appears — three idle panes read at one moment gave two dim suggestions and one genuinely empty box. So emptiness alone distinguishes neither a pane with no suggestion from a pane read too early, nor either from a pane whose occupant simply has nothing pending.
Text in an input box is not the human
An agent cannot run this check on itself: it is working by definition while it looks, so it never sees the idle state it is asking about.
Text in an input box is not the human

One pane carried the same string before and after a working interval with nothing typed in between. That looked like corroboration that a person had left a line sitting there. It is the opposite — an unchanged string across a working interval, with no one at the keyboard, is what a regenerated suggestion looks like. The observation that felt like confirmation was the tell, read backwards.
Text in an input box is not the human

Treating that text as a reason to hold has a cost that never surfaces. A supervisor that will not prompt its own agents does not fail — it quietly absorbs their work into its own context, and from outside it only looks slow. Six panes sat idle here on that mistake, and a seventh agent was started purely to route around one of them.
Text in an input box is not the human
That shape generalizes past input boxes: a safety rule that silently collapses delegation back into the supervisor is worse than no rule, because nothing reports the collapse.
Text in an input box is not the human

Where the text really is the human's, it is still not authorization — a line nobody has pressed enter on is one its writer is free to rewrite or drop. Authority comes from a sent message or from delegated authority over the work. Where neither covers the case, the size of the decision settles it: small and reversible proceeds, while anything that sets a convention or is expensive to undo waits. An entity type with dozens of instances is the second kind.
Text in an input box is not the human
Confirm intent over the cross-session channel, which reaches an agent without touching its box at all.
Text in an input box is not the human
A closed pane is not lost work

Two panes in this workspace were closed before the cleanup started, and what those sessions concluded turned out to be already filed as pages. The check ran against the sessions' own transcripts rather than the panes: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl holds one JSON object per line, and its customTitle field names what the session was about. 86 of those transcripts exist for this graph.
A closed pane is not lost work
So harvest a session while its pane is still open, and read the transcript when one closes first.
A closed pane is not lost work

The graph has no failing build to point at, so the search went to what exists in it that nothing reports: 622 page files under 80 bytes, and nine titles that live both as another page's alias:: value and as their own file of under 80 bytes. pages/Digital Garden.md at zero bytes and pages/AST.md at three are two of the nine.

Aliases and namespaces are why a link can read correctly and still miss — 1,224 of 4,689 pages carry an alias:: line. [[AST]] arrives at Programming/Abstract/Syntax/Tree through its alias, while a plain [[Abstract Syntax Tree]] arrives at a new empty page.

The breaks reach outside the graph too. My/Dotfiles holds logseq:// deep links naming over a hundred pages in this graph, and a rename here is what breaks a link there, with neither side saying so.

Four of those links were reported dead and none of them were. Three name pages whose titles contain spaces, left unencoded in the URL where the rest of the repo uses %20, so any pattern that stops at whitespace truncates the title and calls it missing. The fourth is a URL built from two adjacent string literals on consecutive source lines, so a line-based scan sees only My/AI/Rule/ and reads the rest of the path as absent. The convention was sound the whole time and the scan was wrong, which is the more expensive failure of the two — a false break sends someone to repair what already works.

Two conditions worth suspecting came back clean. No two page titles collide on case alone, and all 34 generated skills under .claude/ carry the same body as their .rulesync/ source once rulesync's own frontmatter keys and its YAML line-wrapping are set aside, so no agent here is reading stale instructions.

Mtime is the wrong instrument for that second check: 18 of the 34 sources are newer than the copy they generate, and one commit wrote both sides in every case sampled, so the ordering is an artifact of checkout write order. Compare the bodies.

First day with the seat in a tmux session rather than a herdr workspace, and the first run as several context windows instead of one — My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Bed Down. No scribe ran, so the journal and the commits sat with the seat.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed

A claim about tmux session names went out having been tested only against targets that named a window explicitly, session:0. That is the single target shape a stray dot in the name leaves alone, so the test passed on everything it was given and confirmed the opposite of the truth. Bare targets — has-session among them — fail on such a name: tmux/Q/Why does a session name containing a dot break every bare -t target?.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed

The falsifier was already written down beside the claim. It cost one command and was not run, which is the same omission as reading an ahead-behind count without fetching first (git/Q/Does an ahead-behind count against origin reflect the remote's current state?) and as calling a capability absent after four refusals. None of the three lacked evidence; all three had it one command away.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed
So a rule that holds on every sample tried is not yet a finding. Look for the sample that would break it, and if none can be constructed, say which inputs were tried.
A test can pass on every input that could not have failed
An absence is a dated claim, not a property

A seat met four refusals on claude --chrome, recorded the capability as unavailable, and after bedding down ran the identical command successfully first try. Meanwhile the fleet had a source written down as blocked when only one route to it was — the constraint belonged to the fallback tool, not to the thing being reached. My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Browser now leads with the route that works.
An absence is a dated claim, not a property

Bedding down is therefore a retry, and the useful shape for an absence is the shape of a count: what was tried, when, and what the failure looked like. Written as a property, an absence never gets retested, because nothing about it says it might have expired.
An absence is a dated claim, not a property
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Logseq/Journal and Logseq/Journal/Editorial headings instruct topic-led narrative blocks above the change log. Person/codekiln deleted three such blocks from their own journal on 2026-08-18 Tue and has written none since; 08-16, 08-18 and 08-19 are change log only. Following the pages put five of them into today's journal before the record of that deletion was read.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Neither source is wrong about what it says. The page says what the practice was, the journals say what it is, and the page carries no date, so nothing on its face marks it as the older one. What settled it was reading the last four journals rather than reasoning about which kind of source ought to win.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs

Where a page and an observed human action disagree, the action decides the immediate question and the disagreement is worth filing rather than quietly obeying one side. Changing a convention page is not the reading agent's call; noticing that it teaches something nobody does any longer is.
A governing page can be out of date and still governs
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository

The fleet's conventions held that tmp/ is gitignored, and reasoned from it: that working notes there are private, and that git add -f on such a file bypasses a secret scan. In this garden .gitignore carries no tmp rule at all, three notes under tmp/ are tracked, and anything written there is published. The warned-of bypass does not exist here, and neither does the privacy it assumed.
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository

A claim of that shape reads as being about the harness when it is really about one checkout, so it travels intact and arrives false. git check-ignore answers it per repository in one call. My/AI/Agent/Fleet now asks the question rather than carrying the answer.
A convention claim stops being true when it crosses a repository
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal

The seat's session was ls-encode-garden, then hayward-ls-encode-garden, then hayward-2026-08-24, then hayward-2026-08-24-LEG — two of those changes on one day. Every page naming the current one as a literal was wrong within days of being written, and a successor reading it has no way to tell a stale literal from a live one.
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal

The repair is to name the scheme where the scheme is decided and to name the command that reads the live value, tmux display-message -p '#{session_name}'. A page describing a pattern survives the next rename; a page quoting a value has to be found and edited.
A name that has changed four times should not be written as a literal
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce

A peer seat committed into this shared checkout mid-task, and the seat's own next commit landed on top of theirs without either noticing. Nothing collided, because both stage named paths; git add -A at that moment would have swept up work in flight. The 2026-08-18 Tue entry on My/AI/Agent/Chief of Staff/Scribe reached this conclusion with a scribe present to enforce it — today it held with no scribe at all, which is the stronger form of the same evidence.
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce
It follows that default-branch, in-sync and tree-clean are readings of a moment in any shared checkout, and a report saying so should say when it was read.
The rule that held was the one nobody was awake to enforce
The morning, and what it produced

Three context windows, the third taking the seat at 11:55 and closing the morning at codekiln's wrap. CursorAI/Explanation/Grok Bot on a Teams seat filed from a worker that ran 8m 4s; archive.ph updated with a result Person/codekiln tested themselves; the fleet's browser rule filed on My/AI/Agent/Fleet/Browser; the display swept twice. Every commit pushed, no worker left running, and no window left open past its commit.
The morning, and what it produced

The seat also answered a peer's search of this graph — whether it already held a note on getting past Medium's login wall. It did: one page, ten months old, never revisited since the day it was written.
The morning, and what it produced
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution

The Grok Bot brief expected the product name to be a voice-input mis-transcription of Cursor's Bugbot, and told the worker to stop and ask rather than choose between that and xAI's Grok. Neither guess was needed. The product is real under the name as heard, with its own Cursor documentation, and the worker settled it from a primary source before writing a line.
A brief's hedge can be wrong in the direction of caution
